Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the introduction to a guide for a REST API that manages calendar bookings. Around 200 words.

This API manages calendar bookings across one or more calendars, and covers creation, reading, updates, and cancellations. It handles time zones, recurrence rules, and availability checks, and returns conflicts when a requested slot overlaps an existing booking.

Each booking belongs to a calendar and carries a start time, end time, and a list of attendees. You can query bookings by date range, filter by calendar or attendee, and subscribe to webhooks for creation, update, and cancellation events. No two confirmed bookings on the same calendar can overlap; the API enforces this rule everywhere.

Authentication uses bearer tokens scoped to a single calendar, or an organization-wide key with access to every calendar under it. Read endpoints allow 100 requests per minute per token; write endpoints allow 20. Exceeding a limit returns a 429 with a Retry-After header. The sections that follow cover authentication, the booking lifecycle, recurrence and exceptions, availability queries, webhooks, and error codes, each with example requests in curl and a reference table of fields and their constraints.

If you are integrating a scheduling widget or a two-way calendar sync, start with the availability and booking endpoints. Those cover most use cases on their own.

output:
You send a request to a URL and get data back. This API works the same way, using plain web requests to manage calendar bookings.

A booking is an appointment on a calendar: it has a start time, an end time, and a list of attendees. You create one by sending a request with those details; the API checks whether the time slot is free and either confirms the booking or tells you it conflicts with an existing one. No two confirmed bookings on the same calendar can overlap.

To prove you're allowed to make a request, you include a bearer token, a text string that acts like a password, with each call. A token can cover one calendar or, if it's an organization key, every calendar in the organization. You get 100 requests per minute for reading bookings and 20 per minute for creating, changing, or canceling them. Send more than that and you get an error telling you how long to wait before trying again.

Beyond creating and canceling bookings, you can look them up by date range, calendar, or attendee, and you can ask the API to notify your own server when a booking is created, changed, or canceled, instead of checking repeatedly. Later sections walk through each of these with example requests you can copy and run.
